To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the IGF2R has multiple binding sites for IGF-II and PMP-BSAs, that the cancer-associated IGF2R mutants have altered binding to IGF-II but not PMP, and that the Gln-1454 → His mutation undergoes a time-dependent loss in IGF-II binding.

five missense mutations in the extracellular domain of the human insulin-like growth factor-II receptor (IGF-II/M6PR) were identified in human cancers; four of these mutants demonstrated alterations in ligand binding to IGF-II/M6PR; the Ile-1571 → Thr mutation completely eliminated ligand binding to the receptor; and the Gly-1449 Val mutant exhibited a time-dependent loss in IGF-II binding that was not observed with the wild-type IGF-II/Mannose
the IGF2R plays an important role in regulating cell proliferation and that several missense mutations in the IGF2Receptor have been identified in various human cancers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the insulin-like growth factor-II/mannose 5-phosphate receptor ( IGF2R ) and its function in human cancers.
understanding how mutations of the IGF2R gene can contribute to the development of cancer and the role of the IGF system in the development of cancer.
the identification and characterization of cancer-associated missense mutations in human IGF2R and the effects these mutations have upon the binding of IGF-II and PMP-BSAs to IGF2R.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cancer-associated mutations of the IGF2R extracytoplasm domain result in a decrease of ligand binding.
cancer-associated missense IGF-2R mutations can alter ligand binding, and this is likely to be a contributing mechanism in the increased cell proliferation seen in these cancers.

the mutations in the IGF2R gene in human cancers are associated with loss-of-function mutations that result in a loss or reduction of the IGF-II binding sites on the IGF2 receptor, and this loss of binding sites is the mechanism by which the IGF2 mutations cause cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer-associated missense IGF 2R mutations disrupt IGF2R functions that are dependent on ligand binding.
the mutations of the IGF2R that have been associated with cancer are associated with loss of function of IGF2 binding.

the Ile-1571 → Thr mutation eliminated binding of the ligand, the Gly-1449 and Cys-1252 mutations decreased the binding affinity of the receptor, the Gln 1445 mutation resulted in a decrease in the number of binding sites and an accelerated dissociation of the ligand from the receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
missense IGF-2R mutants identified in human cancers can have significant effects on the ability of IGF-2Rs to bind IGF-II and mannose 6- phosphate.
cancer-associated missense IGF-2R mutations can alter IGF-2 binding to the receptor.

the IGF2R extracellular domain is a critical component of the receptor's ability to bind ligand, and disruption of this domain by cancer-associated missense mutations can result in a loss of IGF- II binding.
